data.title: approvals list shows the approver class column (RA-why part held by GR-approval-evidence's file)

data.claim: classify(row) separates operator/window/policy/retry/none and flags contradictory markers
data.falsifier: a hand-appended answer with mixed markers is classed as an honest window/operator approval
data.mechanism: policy answers are recorded by record_policy with policy+policy: name+via+source; a person answer passes E.judge
data.probe_output: 14 passed (forged policy flag, forged policy name, unproven level, unregistered rule all flagged)
data.question: Can approver class be derived from the folded ask row alone, with forged markers detected?

chunk_findings.detail: `explain` derives window evidence from the current state/config rather than from the ask row. Given a request that was approved under an earlier standing window, `classify` still returns `class="window"` because the row’s markers are unchanged, but `explain` calls `PO.window_start(state, cfg)` (which is not passed the row or ask id) and uses whatever window is implied by the current state. If that window has ended, the `if start` guards on lines 94-95 return empty `window_start`/`window_expires`; if a newer window has started, the evidence reports the newer window’s start/expiry instead of the one that authorized the request. This violates the stated acceptance that an approval under a standing window reports its rule and expiry, because the evidence is no longer the historical evidence for that approval.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:92-95

chunk_findings.detail: The acceptance criterion says an operator answer must report the transcript attest id, but this test only asserts `w["evidence"]["digest"] == filed.digest`. A `why` implementation that omits any transcript/attest id and returns only the request digest will satisfy the test, so the new tests do not actually enforce the required operator evidence; the wrong output (no attest id) is not refuted by this test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_an_operator_answer_reports_channel_level_and_proof

chunk_findings.detail: `classify` labels every `PO.RULES` hit `window` and `explain` then stamps `window_start` / `window_expires` from `PO.window_start(state, cfg)` (the live window), without checking that `answered_at` falls inside that window. After the standing window rolls, an ask approved under the previous window still reports class `window` and an expiry that does not cover the approval: given `window_start` now `T2`, `standing_window_s` = 3600, and an approved `policy:` row whose `answered_at` is `T2 - 10`, the report shows expiry `T2+3600` and claims the standing window approved it. The module contract says `window` means a standing rule *inside* the standing window; this path never tests that.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:classify

chunk_findings.detail: On the automatic path `classify` writes `E.verified_level(...)` and then overwrites it with `level=1`. `approvals_why` treats that field as verified and, when `claimed_level != 1`, prints `verified L1, answer claims L{claimed}`. Given a policy-channel approval whose stored level is 2 (and whose `verified_level` is 2 or 0), the report states a verification result that was never computed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:55

chunk_findings.detail: The added `**WH.tag(r, cfg)` is placed inside `_commands(state)`, but the diff context shows that helper’s signature as `_commands(state) -> list[dict[str, Any]]`, with no `cfg` parameter, and the manifest shows only four added lines in `audit.py` (no signature or caller changes). When `approvals list` or `log` builds an approval row, evaluating the dict literal references `cfg` before it is bound in that scope, raising `NameError: name 'cfg' is not defined`. If a module-level `cfg` somehow existed, it would still be wrong because it would classify approvals using whatever global config was last loaded rather than the repo-specific config passed to the API.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/audit.py:64

chunk_findings.detail: `classify` labels an answer as `window` based only on the policy markers and the rule id in `answered_by`, and `explain` then fills the window evidence from `PO.window_start(state, cfg)` at read time. It never uses `row["answered_at"]` to identify or validate the standing window that was active when the approval happened. For example, if a request was approved at epoch `1000` under a window that started at `1000` and expired at `4600`, but a later standing window starts at epoch `9000`, `explain` for the old ask returns `window_start` `9000` and `window_expires` `12600`. That is false evidence: the approval is reported under a window that did not exist at answer time, and an approval outside the returned window is still shown as automatic `window` with no anomaly.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:52, 78-82

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert "operator" not in w["summary"].split("automatic")[0]` only checks text before the first occurrence of `"automatic"`. If `explain` produced a summary such as `"automatic approval by operator"`, the split would be `['', ' approval by operator']`, the checked part would be empty, and the test would pass even though the summary calls an automatic approval operator-approved. This defeats the acceptance requirement that window/policy approvals not be reported as operator-approved.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_a_window_approval_names_the_rule_and_the_window_expiry

chunk_findings.detail: The test name and acceptance criterion require proof via a transcript attest id, but the test only asserts `w["evidence"]["digest"] == filed.digest`. If `explain` returns an operator answer with no transcript attest id field in `evidence`, this test still passes, so it does not verify the required operator-answer evidence.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_an_operator_answer_reports_channel_level_and_proof

chunk_findings.detail: On a fully marked policy/window/retry approval, `classify` stores `E.verified_level(row, cfg)` and then unconditionally overwrites `level` with `1`. `approvals_why` treats `why["level"]` as the verified level (`verified L{why['level']}, answer claims L{why['claimed_level']}`). Given an automatic row whose claim is L2 and whose `verified_level` is 0, the report says the verified level is L1.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:classify

chunk_findings.detail: Window evidence is taken from the live window, not the window that approved the ask: `PO.window_start(state, cfg)` plus `cfg.approvals.standing_window_s`. After a standing-window restart, `approvals why` for an earlier window approval prints the new start and expiry (or blank expiry if `window_start` is now unset) even though those bounds did not cover the approval.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:explain

chunk_findings.detail: The window test claims a report must not call a window approval operator-approved, but `"operator" not in w["summary"].split("automatic")[0]` does not check that. Given summary `"automatic operator-approved via window complete_unavailable"`, the prefix before `"automatic"` is empty, so the assertion passes while the report still says operator-approved. The same check rejects a correct summary such as `"standing window, not operator-approved (automatic)"` because `"operator"` appears before `"automatic"`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:87

chunk_findings.detail: The added line `**WH.tag(r, cfg),` is inside `_commands(state)`, but `_commands` is still declared to take only `state`, and the diff does not add a `cfg` parameter, import, or module-level definition. As written, the first call to `_commands` — for example when `approvals list` or `approvals log` builds audit rows — will raise `NameError: name 'cfg' is not defined` at that line, so the new class/automatic/anomaly audit output cannot be produced.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/audit.py:_commands

chunk_findings.detail: `_window_at` selects the latest prior in-scope policy answer as the window start even when that prior answer's window has already expired. It should only use a prior answer when that prior answer's window still covers the row being explained; otherwise the row itself is the window opener, as the docstring says. For example, with `cfg.approvals.standing_window_s = 3600`, `standing_verbs` containing the verb, and two approved window-rule asks both marked `policy=True`, `via="policy"`, `source="policy"`, `answered_by="policy:window_rule"` where `window_rule` is in `PO.RULES`: ask A has `answered_at=1000`, ask B has `answered_at=4601`. For B, `prior=[1000]`, so `_window_at` returns `start=1000`, `expires=4600`. `explain` then sets the anomaly “the answer falls outside the standing window…” and reports `window_expires` as 4600, even though B should open a new window at 4601 (expiring 8201) and not be anomalous. This misreports legitimate standing-window approvals after a window rolls.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:85-96 (`_window_at`)

chunk_findings.detail: The acceptance criterion requires a standing-window approval to report the window rule id and expiry, but the window tests never assert either. `test_an_old_window_approval_is_not_reported_under_a_later_window` only checks `class`, `automatic`, `anomaly`, and `window_start`; `test_audit_rows_carry_the_class_and_mark_automatic` and `test_the_why_command` only check class/automatic. An implementation returning `class="window"`, `automatic=True`, `evidence={"window_start": ...}` while omitting or blanking `rule` and `window_expires` passes every new test, so the required expiry/rule evidence is not actually enforced.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_an_old_window_approval_is_not_reported_under_a_later_window

chunk_findings.detail: This test does not enforce the “class as a column in list/log” or “policy and window marked automatic” requirements for the audit line. It only asserts `"automatic" in AU.line(row)` for a window row; if `AU.line` emits `"automatic"` but omits the class (`window`), the test still passes even though the log does not show the class column. It also never checks a policy row’s `AU.line`, so a policy approval could be printed without the automatic marker and the suite would not fail.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_audit_rows_carry_the_class_and_mark_automatic

chunk_findings.detail: The non-JSON CLI assertion `assert code == 0 and "none" in out` is too weak to prove the class is reported as `none`. Given a pending request, an implementation could print a message containing the word `none` in an unrelated field, such as `anomaly: none`, while omitting the actual class column, and the test would still pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_the_why_command

chunk_findings.detail: The outside-window guard is dead whenever this ask is the only policy standing-verb row, so a window-rule approval that was not under any standing window is still reported as class `window` with a fabricated covering expiry. `classify` sets `class="window"` solely because `rule in PO.RULES`, and `_window_at` builds `prior` only from other `policy` rows (an operator open is excluded). With `prior` empty, `start = max(prior, default=at)` is this row’s own `answered_at`, so `expires = answered_at + standing_window_s` and `answered_at >= expires` is false for any positive window. Given `standing_window_s` 3600, a real window opened by a non-policy standing answer at T0, and a `policy:` + `PO.RULES` approval at T0+4000, `explain` returns class `window`, `window_start` T0+4000, `window_expires` T0+7600, and no anomaly. The same self-anchor is why the earlier “expiry does not cover this approval / live window rolled” case is not actually detected when no earlier policy standing row exists.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:_window_at

chunk_findings.detail: Acceptance requires a standing-window approval to report the window rule and its expiry, but no test asserts either field. `test_an_old_window_approval_is_not_reported_under_a_later_window` only checks `window_start` and an empty anomaly; `test_audit_rows_carry_the_class_and_mark_automatic` and `test_the_why_command` only check `class == "window"` and `automatic`. A `why` result with class `window`, a start timestamp, and no `rule` / `window_expires` (or an expiry that does not cover `answered_at`) still passes every test here, so the required evidence is not enforced.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:87

chunk_findings.detail: The added row expansion `**WH.tag(r, cfg)` is inside `_commands(state)`, whose signature in the reviewed hunk has no `cfg` parameter and no visible binding for `cfg` in that scope. When `approvals list` or `log` calls `_commands(state)` to build approval rows, Python evaluates the dict literal and attempts to pass `cfg` to `WH.tag`, raising `NameError: name 'cfg' is not defined` (or `TypeError` if a caller was changed to pass `cfg` but the unchanged helper still accepts only `state`). This breaks the required class column in list/log output.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/audit.py:64

chunk_findings.detail: `_window_at` chooses the latest prior standing fire unconditionally (`start = max(prior, default=at)`) and then `explain` flags the row if `answered_at >= expires`. That treats an expired prior fire as the window that was open, instead of letting the current approval open a new window. For example, with `cfg.approvals.standing_window_s=3600`, if a prior ask A answered at epoch `1000` by a non-retry standing policy rule is still present, and a later ask B answered at epoch `5000` has the same window markers, `prior` contains `1000`, so `explain(B)` reports `window_start` for `1000` and `window_expires` for `4600` and sets the anomaly “the answer falls outside the standing window…”, even though B opened a new standing window and should report start `5000`, expiry `8600`, and no anomaly. This violates the acceptance requirement that a standing-window approval report the window that approved it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:_window_at

chunk_findings.detail: This is the only test that exercises standing-window evidence, but it never asserts the required `rule` id or `expiry`. If `W.explain` returns `{"class": "window", "automatic": True, "anomaly": "", "evidence": {"window_start": ...}}` with no `expiry` field, or with an expiry that does not match the window, the assertions still pass: the test only checks `anomaly == ""`, `window_start == W._iso(at)`, and later anomaly behavior. The CLI and audit tests likewise only check `class`/`automatic`. Thus the suite can pass even though `approvals why` omits the window rule and expiry required by the acceptance.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_an_old_window_approval_is_not_reported_under_a_later_window

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten tests no longer enforce that automatic window/policy reports avoid calling the approval operator-approved; they only require `row["automatic"] is True` and the substring `"automatic"` in `AU.line(row)`. Given a wrong implementation whose summary is `"operator-approved via window complete_unavailable (automatic)"`, the window tests still pass (`class == "window"`, `automatic is True`, evidence checks pass) and this audit test still passes because the line contains `"automatic"`. That violates the stated acceptance that policy and window approvals be marked automatic so a report does not call them operator-approved.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_audit_rows_carry_the_class_and_mark_automatic

chunk_findings.detail: `**WH.tag(r, cfg)` is still evaluated inside `_commands(state)`, whose signature in this diff is `_commands(state) -> list[dict[str, Any]]` with no `cfg` parameter and no caller or signature edit. Building an `approvals list` or `log` row therefore hits `NameError: name 'cfg' is not defined` before any approval class can be attached. The earlier finding is unanswered: the same four-line addition still names an unbound `cfg`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/audit.py:64

chunk_findings.detail: `_window_at` never sees the approval that actually opened the standing window, and it treats every earlier policy row on a standing verb as a new window start. The scan requires `r["policy"]`, so an operator answer that opened the window (policy false) is dropped; with no other policy rows, `max(prior, default=at)` sets start to this row’s own `answered_at`. Given an operator standing-verb approval at epoch 1000 (window 1000–4600) and a window approval at 2000, the report’s evidence is start 2000 / expiry 5600, and `answered_at >= expires` is `2000 >= 5600`, so the out-of-window anomaly never fires. After a later operator window at 9000 and a window approval at 9500, a leftover policy row at 2000 is still `<= 9500`, so start stays 2000, expiry 5600, and the 9500 approval is falsely flagged as outside the window that covered it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:86

chunk_findings.detail: The acceptance case that a standing-window approval must report the window rule and its expiry is not asserted anywhere in this file. `test_an_old_window_approval_is_not_reported_under_a_later_window` only checks `anomaly` and `evidence["window_start"]`; `test_audit_rows_carry_the_class_and_mark_automatic` only checks `class == "window"` and that the word `automatic` appears; `test_the_why_command` only checks `class` and `automatic`. An `explain` result for `complete_unavailable` that omits `rule`, omits expiry, or fills expiry from a later live window still passes every assertion here.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:90

This is the same gap as previous finding #4; the added no-operator check does not address it.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier gap is only half closed. `AU.line` is still checked only for a window row, and only for the substrings `"automatic"` and not `"operator"`. A line such as `automatic via policy` with no class token still passes, so `approvals list` / `approvals log` can omit the class column. A policy-rule row is never passed to `AU.line`, so that path can still print operator wording and the suite will not fail. Given a policy approval whose audit line is `approved by operator`, `test_audit_rows_carry_the_class_and_mark_automatic` stays green.

chunk_findings.detail: `_window_at` chooses the latest prior standing fire unconditionally (`start = max(prior, default=at)`) and then `explain` flags the row if `answered_at >= expires`. That treats an expired prior fire as the window that was open, instead of letting the current approval open a new window. For example, with `cfg.approvals.standing_window_s=3600`, if a prior ask A answered at epoch `1000` by a non-retry standing policy rule is still present, and a later ask B answered at epoch `5000` has the same window markers, `prior` contains `1000`, so `explain(B)` reports `window_start` for `1000` and `window_expires` for `4600` and sets the anomaly “the answer falls outside the standing window…”, even though B opened a new standing window and should report start `5000`, expiry `8600`, and no anomaly. This violates the acceptance requirement that a standing-window approval report the window that approved it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:_window_at

chunk_findings.detail: This is the only test that exercises standing-window evidence, but it never asserts the required `rule` id or `expiry`. If `W.explain` returns `{"class": "window", "automatic": True, "anomaly": "", "evidence": {"window_start": ...}}` with no `expiry` field, or with an expiry that does not match the window, the assertions still pass: the test only checks `anomaly == ""`, `window_start == W._iso(at)`, and later anomaly behavior. The CLI and audit tests likewise only check `class`/`automatic`. Thus the suite can pass even though `approvals why` omits the window rule and expiry required by the acceptance.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_an_old_window_approval_is_not_reported_under_a_later_window

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten tests no longer enforce that automatic window/policy reports avoid calling the approval operator-approved; they only require `row["automatic"] is True` and the substring `"automatic"` in `AU.line(row)`. Given a wrong implementation whose summary is `"operator-approved via window complete_unavailable (automatic)"`, the window tests still pass (`class == "window"`, `automatic is True`, evidence checks pass) and this audit test still passes because the line contains `"automatic"`. That violates the stated acceptance that policy and window approvals be marked automatic so a report does not call them operator-approved.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:test_audit_rows_carry_the_class_and_mark_automatic

chunk_findings.detail: `**WH.tag(r, cfg)` is still evaluated inside `_commands(state)`, whose signature in this diff is `_commands(state) -> list[dict[str, Any]]` with no `cfg` parameter and no caller or signature edit. Building an `approvals list` or `log` row therefore hits `NameError: name 'cfg' is not defined` before any approval class can be attached. The earlier finding is unanswered: the same four-line addition still names an unbound `cfg`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/audit.py:64

chunk_findings.detail: `_window_at` never sees the approval that actually opened the standing window, and it treats every earlier policy row on a standing verb as a new window start. The scan requires `r["policy"]`, so an operator answer that opened the window (policy false) is dropped; with no other policy rows, `max(prior, default=at)` sets start to this row’s own `answered_at`. Given an operator standing-verb approval at epoch 1000 (window 1000–4600) and a window approval at 2000, the report’s evidence is start 2000 / expiry 5600, and `answered_at >= expires` is `2000 >= 5600`, so the out-of-window anomaly never fires. After a later operator window at 9000 and a window approval at 9500, a leftover policy row at 2000 is still `<= 9500`, so start stays 2000, expiry 5600, and the 9500 approval is falsely flagged as outside the window that covered it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/why.py:86

chunk_findings.detail: The acceptance case that a standing-window approval must report the window rule and its expiry is not asserted anywhere in this file. `test_an_old_window_approval_is_not_reported_under_a_later_window` only checks `anomaly` and `evidence["window_start"]`; `test_audit_rows_carry_the_class_and_mark_automatic` only checks `class == "window"` and that the word `automatic` appears; `test_the_why_command` only checks `class` and `automatic`. An `explain` result for `complete_unavailable` that omits `rule`, omits expiry, or fills expiry from a later live window still passes every assertion here.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_why.py:90

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertion `assert (body["why"]["rule"] == "complete_unavailable" and body["why"]["evidence"]["window_expires"])` does not verify the expiry value; it only checks that `window_expires` is truthy. Given a CLI JSON result where `body["why"]["evidence"]["window_expires"]` is `"1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"` or any other non-empty incorrect string, the test still passes because the `and` expression evaluates to that string and `assert` only tests truthiness. This allows a CLI-side expiry bug to pass the test even though the acceptance criterion is that a standing-window approval report the correct expiry.
